sections.title: The ground, the air, the clothes

cues.sentence: It's two in the morning.
Something creaks near your front door.
Your eyes open.
You lie still and listen.
There it is again.
A small, dry sound from the hallway.
You get out of bed, cross the room and check the lock.
It's secure.
You stand there another moment, looking into the dark, until the sound comes again.
It's the floor.
You were the one making it.
You go back to bed, slightly annoyed with yourself, and pull the covers up.
The door is locked.
The walls are solid.
Eventually, you close your eyes.
Now take away the lock.
Take away the door.
Take away the quiet room, the mattress, the blanket, and the light switch beside your bed.
How would you sleep?
For much of human history, darkness arrived without a key to turn.
But that didn't mean people simply collapsed wherever they stood and hoped for the best.
To understand the night, first look at the world around them.
Two hundred thousand years ago, in what is now southern Africa, daylight moves across a rocky slope.
Grasses bend in the breeze.
Beyond them are patches of bush and open woodland, with trees scattered across the landscape.
As the sun drops, the rocks hold a little warmth.
The shadows stretch.
The paths through the vegetation become harder to see.
Near a broad shelter in the cliff, a community gathers.
Adults return from different tasks.
Children move between them.
Grass is carried into the shelter; hands clear a space on the ground.
At the edge of the gathering, people settle near the warmth of a fire.
There is movement everywhere.
Somebody shifts closer to the light.
Someone else makes room.
A child is reluctant to settle; an adult draws them close.
The day hasn't ended all at once just because the sun has gone down.
The precise size of any particular ancient group is difficult to know.
But the archaeological traces at one South African site give us a remarkable glimpse of a place people returned to: Border Cave,
in the Lebombo Mountains.
And at the back of that shelter, archaeologists found something unexpectedly familiar.
A bed.
Or, more precisely, traces of many layers of bedding.
The remains are subtle now: ancient fragments of broad-leaved grass, identified by careful analysis.
Some bedding at Border Cave dates to around two hundred thousand years ago.
Imagine the preparation before nightfall.
Grass gathered in bundles, carried back to the shelter and spread where people could rest.
A softer surface between a body and the ground.
Not a mattress with a warranty.
But certainly better than finding a sharp stone with your back at three in the morning.
The grass wasn't the only thing underfoot.
Researchers also found layers of ash associated with the bedding.
Sometimes that ash appears to have come from older bedding that had burned.
Why place fresh grass over ash?
One possibility is that it helped create a cleaner, insulated base.
The researchers also suggested the fine ash might have discouraged crawling pests.
That part is an interpretation, not a label left behind by the people who made it.
But it points to a problem that is easy to overlook.
The danger of the night wasn't only something large moving beyond the fire.
It could be something small enough to disappear into the bedding.
Tiny stone fragments were found among the grass as well.
The same surface that offered somewhere to rest may also have been a place to sit and work.
A sleeping place.
A working place.
A piece of the landscape brought indoors, if a shelter can be called indoors.
But a bed still leaves one problem unsolved.
What happens beyond the edge of the light?
At Border Cave, evidence of fires appears through a long sequence of occupations.
For the people using such a place, a fire could offer warmth and light.
In some circumstances it might also help discourage animals from approaching.
But it could not turn night into day.
And it was never a guarantee that nothing would come near.
Picture the firelight reaching the people nearest it: faces, hands, the pale edges of grass.
Farther back, rock disappears into shadow.
Beyond the shelter mouth, the light weakens until the bushes are only shapes.
The surrounding world doesn't stop when people settle down.
Wind passes through dry stems.
Insects continue their work.
Somewhere beyond the slope, an animal moves through vegetation.
A sound can travel a long way in the dark.
Its owner might be harmless.
Or not.
From inside the shelter, the difference isn't always obvious.
People could choose where to rest, use the shelter and tend a fire, but even a carefully prepared place had limits.
Smoke could irritate.
A change in weather could bring cold or rain.
A sleeping person still had to let go of attention for hours.
And that's the strange bargain at the heart of every night: to recover from the day,
they had to become less aware of the world around them.
So what if a sound came from the grass outside?
Imagine a scrape beyond the shelter.
Then silence.
Then the sound again.
Inside, not everyone responds in the same way.
Some remain asleep.
Others lift their heads.
Eyes turn toward the entrance, where the firelight ends.
In daylight, a moving branch is just a moving branch.
At night, with the source hidden, it can hold a whole collection of possibilities.
A gust of wind.
A small animal.
Something larger.
The scrape stops.
The night continues.
People settle again, but perhaps not all at the same moment.
It's easy to picture one assigned guard standing at the entrance until sunrise.
And it's possible that groups used watches in some situations.
But an ancient layer of grass cannot tell us that a guard stood there every night.
There is another possibility.
A group does not need to move through the night like a single creature, sleeping and waking at exactly the same time.
Researchers have found a striking example of that among people living today.
In a study in Tanzania,
researchers used wrist-worn activity monitors to estimate the sleep of thirty-three Hadza
adults over twenty nights.
The Hadza are a living community with their own history; the study tells us about its participants,
not a direct record of ancient sleep.
The researchers found that the monitored adults were all estimated to be asleep at the same time during only
eighteen one-minute intervals across the study.
Eighteen minutes across twenty nights, not eighteen minutes every night.
Their sleep overlapped, but it didn't line up perfectly.
Some people fell asleep later.
Some woke earlier.
Some were active during the night for reasons of their own.
Researchers have proposed that differences in sleeping times could sometimes give a group more opportunities to notice a threat.
This idea is known as the sentinel hypothesis.
Notice the difference between the observation and the explanation.
The monitors estimated whether people were asleep or active; they did not prove that every awake person was keeping watch.
And the study cannot establish exactly how people slept at Border Cave.
Still, it opens up a different way to think about the night.
A sleeping community isn't necessarily a room where every pair of eyes closes at once.
Back at the shelter, the fire has burned lower.
The space nearest the entrance is darker now.
Beyond it, the landscape is still moving.
And the next challenge might be closer than the bushes.
Even without a threat outside, a night on the ground takes preparation.
The surface beneath the body matters.
So do the air, the wind, the heat of the fire, and the space around other sleepers.
Some may want to be near the warmth.
Others may shift away when the smoke changes direction.
People make room, adjust their positions and settle again.
A crowded place can be reassuring; it can also be full of elbows.
And what did they wear against the night air?
Clothing is difficult to trace this far back because materials such as skin and plant fibre usually decay.
The exact garments worn at Border Cave are not known.
There are later clues elsewhere.
At a cave in Morocco,
researchers found bone tools and marks on animal bones dating to roughly ninety to one hundred and twenty thousand years ago.
Together, they suggest people processed hides and fur; clothing is one possible use, though not the only one.
That discovery is from a different place and a later time.
It doesn't tell us the cut or appearance of anyone's clothing at Border Cave.
What it does show is how much thought can be hidden inside an ordinary material.
A skin, a length of plant fibre, a layer of grass: each could have many possible uses.
Which of them were used on one particular night is a harder question.
The people at the shelter have another few hours before dawn.
The fire settles.
The ground cools.
Around them, some sleep deeply; others may wake, shift and lie down again.
Then the darkness begins to change.
At first, the shelter mouth is only a paler shape against the rock.
Then the surrounding grasses begin to separate from the shadows.
The outlines of trees return.
The land that seemed so uncertain in the dark becomes visible again, one detail at a time.
The community stirs.
People rise from the grass, step around one another and move toward the day.
The place that held sleepers through the night becomes a place for work and movement again.
Long after those people were gone, traces remained: grass and ash, signs of fire, and small fragments of worked stone.
They cannot tell us every sound of the night or the exact way the community responded to it.
But they offer a different picture from the idea that ancient people simply lay down in the dark and took their chances.
They could prepare a place.
They could use the landscape.
They could be near other people.
And, even then, the night could surprise them.
Back in your room, the floor creaks again.
This time, you know what made it.
You check the door once more anyway, return to bed, and let the quiet settle.
The surroundings have changed.
The question hasn't.
Can you go back to sleep?
